title: The mystics, looking back
hook: the hazelnut, the castle, the dark night, the pots
tomorrow: what does a choir from three churches sound like?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two houses in one storm, and the doing that holds: build on rock. Today, people who spent their lives on where God is found.

Some people pray best with the door shut and the phone in another room. Others think most clearly with their hands in dishwater. Christian mystics answer it more than one way: a hazelnut, a castle, a dark night, a kitchen full of pots. So is God found in the quiet room, or in the dishes? Two answers, both old, both Christian.
screen: `THE SHUT DOOR, OR THE SINK?` → `A HAZELNUT, A CASTLE, A NIGHT, THE POTS.` → `TWO ANSWERS, BOTH OLD.`

segments.voice: View one: go in. Teresa of Ávila pictured the soul as a castle of clear crystal with many rooms, and God in the innermost one; prayer is the door, room by room. John of the Cross wrote of a dark night, when prayer goes dry, and treated even that as part of the way in. Luke has a scene on this side: Martha's sister Mary sits at Jesus's feet, listening, and Jesus says, “Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.” View two: stay in the kitchen. Brother Lawrence, a lay brother working among the pots and pans, said he could keep God company in the noise and clatter of the work as well as on his knees. His side can point to Paul: “whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.” Each side has a fair case, and some Christians keep both: a quiet hour that spills into the work. And underneath both, a woman who saw something small. Julian of Norwich wrote that God showed her a little thing, the size of a hazelnut, in the palm of her hand. She wondered how it could last, and understood: it lasts because God loves it. Here's the detail to tell a friend. Her line “all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well,” comes while she's asking hard questions about sin and pain, not instead of asking them.
screen: `VIEW ONE: THE CASTLE, ROOM BY ROOM.` · `VIEW TWO: GOD AMONG THE POTS.` · `UNDER BOTH: A HAZELNUT, HELD.` · `ASKED IN THE HARD QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `ALL SHALL BE WELL.`

segments.voice: Rest one small thing in your open palm: a nut, a button, a coin. Look at how small it is, and let Julian's question come: how does it last? Then let her answer sit beside it. If you pray, say her line slowly, all shall be well, and leave it there.
The mystics. Christians who wrote about God's nearness, some going inward, some through the dark, one at the kitchen sink.
Carry this: all shall be well, said with the hard questions still open. Day seventeen sixty, done.

howItsDone: Christians read the mystics slowly, often a few lines at a time, and some take up Brother Lawrence's practice of turning to God in the middle of ordinary work.

fork.setup: a friend says, "God is only really found in silent prayer, alone." give the best case for the other side.
options: silence is boring, so busy people shouldn't bother with it.
Julian of Norwich said that prayer doesn't really matter.
Brother Lawrence kept God company among the pots, and Paul says whatsoever ye do, do all to God's glory.
fork.reveal: the other side's best case is the kitchen: Brother Lawrence, and Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:31. her side has Teresa's castle and Mary at Jesus's feet. some keep both.

chat.says: so tired of deciding. pop says sit quiet and pray. choir director says just practice, it'll come. who's right?
options: Maybe both. Teresa went inward; Brother Lawrence found God at the sink. Pray, then practice.
Only the quiet counts. Practicing music is just a distraction from real prayer.
Skip the sitting. Doing the work is the only thing God actually cares about.
chat.meaning: Christian mystics found God both ways: inward, room by room (Teresa), and in the clatter of a kitchen (Brother Lawrence). Some keep both.

Teresa of Ávila.meaning: a Spanish nun who wrote about prayer as a castle

John of the Cross.meaning: a Spanish friar who wrote of the dark night

Brother Lawrence.meaning: a lay brother who practiced God's presence in a kitchen

Julian of Norwich.meaning: an English woman who wrote down her visions of God's love

Martha.meaning: Mary's sister, busy serving when Jesus visited
